document_title: Utqiagvik Observers and an Arctic Ocean Model
post_copy:
Validation is what science does to data to decide if it is good enough. A paper published September 18th inverts that.

Did the model fail? No. It generally caught seasonal timing, especially the end of open water.

Where did it break? During the 2019 marine heatwave the model had ice freezing up earlier than the ocean did. The records cover more than 1,500 km of coast and show late freeze-up and storms that made hunting hard. That fall Utqiagvik took one bowhead, against past fall harvests of up to about 30.

The paper's line is that Indigenous Knowledge "does not require validation by scientific frameworks". Observers are co-authors.

The deck holds a season disc broken open where the records disagree, the observer's October 1st, 2019 entry, and ten author slots.

When a model and a coastline disagree about the same week, which one gets corrected?

#SeaIce #OceanModeling #ArcticAlaska

aftercare: This draft is dated Saturday September 19th, which is the weakest slot of the week. Hold it for Tuesday September 22nd through Thursday the 24th, 8 to 11am AKT, and post it on whichever of those mornings is clear.
Paste the source block as the FIRST comment within 60 seconds of posting, with all four raw URLs intact as plain text. A hyperlink-only paste loses the link on LinkedIn.
Stay on the post for the first 90 minutes and reply to every comment, including the one-word ones. The ask on slide 09 is a real question and the replies are where it earns its saves.

Expect the reading that the model is bad. It is not what the paper says. The reply is slide 07 and C17, that the model generally captured the timing of seasonal changes, especially the end of the open water season, and that a model broadly right is exactly the kind nobody audits.

Expect someone to ask how big the freeze-up error was, in days or in kilometres of ice. The paper publishes a direction and no magnitude, and the deck withholds it on purpose. Say that plainly and don't estimate a number in a comment.
Check saves, comments and dwell at 48 hours and note them against the run, since the one-whale frame and the empty dimension field are both new devices for this page.
editor_notes_for_email: Three things to know before this one goes up. First, the deck prints no magnitude anywhere for the freeze-up error, and that is deliberate rather than an omission. The paper, published September 18th, states only the direction, that in 2019 the model had sea ice freezing up earlier than it actually did, and it publishes no figure for the size of that gap. Slide 02 draws the withholding as a declared break with an empty dimension field. If a reader asks how many days, the honest answer is that the number is not in the paper. Second, the one whale on slide 06 is set against fall harvests of up to about 30. That 30 is a ceiling on past FALL harvests, never an annual average, and the spring hunt is a separate season that is not in the count. The frame says so and any reply should repeat it. Third, no individual in this deck is identified as Indigenous. Billy Adams appears on slide 03 only as an AAOKH observer in Utqiagvik, which is what the UAF release supports. The paper says Indigenous observers are co-authors without saying which of the ten, so a reply that assigns identity to a named author goes past the record.
